title: Digital forensics and investigative questions
concept: Forensics reconstructs activity from digital artifacts while preserving provenance and uncertainty. Incident response also prioritizes containment and recovery; these goals can require different actions.
prepare: Define the question, authorized evidence sources, time window, retention needs and who may access the evidence. Assign a case identifier and record each action.
workflow: Start with an evidence inventory, document the original state, preserve acquired material and examine working copies. Tie every conclusion to an artifact and its interpretation.
limits: A tool finding is not automatically proof of an actor, intent or exact event sequence. Absence of an artifact may reflect incomplete acquisition or retention.
tools: Use a case notebook and evidence worksheet before selecting Autopsy, Volatility or a packet analyzer.

title: Evidence handling and chain of custody
concept: Chain of custody records who handled an item, when, why and how its identity and storage were controlled. A hash is one integrity aid, not a complete custody record.
prepare: Record the source description, acquisition method, operator, start/end times, clock assumptions, storage location, transfers and tool versions. Keep secrets and personal data out of public reports.
workflow: Label original acquisitions, working copies and derived exports separately. Verify hashes at meaningful transfer points and record discrepancies without overwriting the prior record.
limits: A matching digest establishes byte equality relative to the compared digest; it does not authenticate the original source, prove lawful collection or establish what happened before acquisition.
tools: Use SHA-256 manifests, controlled storage and access records. The supplied manifest is a teaching baseline, not a signed provenance statement.

title: Live, logical and physical acquisition
concept: A logical acquisition collects selected accessible objects; a physical image can capture addressable storage sectors. Live collection can preserve volatile state but changes the running system.
prepare: Choose the acquisition method based on the question, encryption state, volatility and operational constraints. Use appropriately validated write protection for offline media where applicable.
workflow: Document the chosen method and unavoidable effects. Preserve the acquisition output and examine a copy using an appropriate parser. Record unreadable areas and acquisition errors.
limits: Do not assume powering off is always best: volatile state and decrypted access can be lost. Conversely, live collection cannot promise zero system changes. SSD TRIM and encryption can limit recovery.
tools: Acquisition utilities and write blockers need separate hardware/media and tested procedures. This handbook does not image the user disk or collect live memory.

title: Disk structures and file-system artifacts
concept: A disk image may contain a partition table; a file-system image may begin directly with a file system. File names, metadata records and file content are different evidence objects.
prepare: Identify image format, sector size and partition layout before selecting an offset. Record the exact parser and options used.
workflow: Use a partition listing, inspect the intended file system, list names and metadata, then export a selected artifact to a separate analysis directory. Preserve the source image unchanged.
limits: An offset copied from another image can produce false errors or wrong interpretation. Sector offsets and byte offsets are not interchangeable. A parser failure does not prove encryption or corruption.
tools: The Sleuth Kit mmls, fsstat, fls and icat support these steps on compatible images. Autopsy provides a graphical case workflow.

title: Deleted files, carving and recovery limits
concept: Deletion often changes allocation or name metadata; content may remain until overwritten or discarded. Carving searches content patterns without relying on the original directory structure.
prepare: Work on a verified image copy and use a separate output directory. Record what the chosen method can reconstruct and whether fragments are expected.
workflow: Compare metadata-based recovery with carved results. Validate file structure and correlate any recovered content with other artifacts. Treat extracted files as untrusted.
limits: A carved file may lack its original name, path or timestamps. Signature matches can be false positives, and absence of recovered data is not proof that a file never existed.
tools: Autopsy, Sleuth Kit and PhotoRec serve different recovery workflows. Recovered objects should be hashed and examined without executing them.

title: File identification and metadata
concept: Extensions, embedded metadata and file-system timestamps describe different aspects of a file. Metadata can be changed, omitted or inherited during copying.
prepare: Record the original source, acquisition context and timezone assumptions. Inspect bytes and format before trusting the filename.
workflow: Compare file identification with parsed metadata. Preserve the raw value and the interpreted value when creating a report. Correlate a timestamp with a second independent artifact.
limits: An image date is not necessarily the time of an observed event. A string match does not prove that text was executed or displayed. File access times can change during handling depending on the environment.
tools: file, strings and ExifTool help triage copies. Use ExifTool read commands; writing metadata would change evidence.

title: Operating-system, browser and application artifacts
concept: Logs, registry data, browser databases and application records describe different layers of activity and may have different retention or clock behavior.
prepare: Identify the source application/version and acquisition completeness. Preserve related SQLite WAL and SHM files when relevant rather than assuming the main database is the complete state.
workflow: Parse a working copy, preserve original event fields and record parser errors. Correlate a browser download record with file-system and network evidence where available.
limits: A history entry does not necessarily establish who physically used the device. Missing records may reflect retention, synchronization, private browsing or an incomplete collection.
tools: Autopsy and platform-specific parsers can extract artifacts; raw source inspection and a second parser help validate critical findings.

title: Memory forensics
concept: Memory can contain process state, loaded modules, network structures and other transient artifacts. A memory image is a time-bound acquisition, not a complete history.
prepare: Record operating system/build, acquisition tool, time and known collection effects. Preserve the dump and prepare required symbols in the analysis environment.
workflow: Begin with image information and a process listing. Correlate suspicious entries with parent relationships, executable metadata, mappings and other evidence before assigning meaning.
limits: A process name alone is not proof of malware. Different enumeration methods can disagree for legitimate or malicious reasons. Missing symbols or unsupported images can invalidate output.
tools: Volatility 3 analyzes supported images. The workbook offers information and process-list commands only; no memory acquisition or credential extraction is performed.

title: Network forensics
concept: A capture contains packets visible at one observation point. Logs from DNS, proxies and firewalls add context but may summarize rather than preserve full traffic.
prepare: Record capture location, clock, filter, start/end times and loss indicators. Protect real captures because they may contain private content and credentials.
workflow: Work from a saved trace, reconstruct relevant conversations and correlate timestamps with host/application records. Record whether payloads are actually visible or inferred from metadata.
limits: Encryption limits plaintext visibility; asymmetric capture and packet loss limit reconstruction. An address alone does not reliably identify a person or physical device.
tools: Wireshark and TShark review saved captures. Refer to the network workbook for creating a synthetic loopback trace.

title: Timeline construction and clock uncertainty
concept: A timeline orders interpreted timestamps, not necessarily causal events. Sources may use UTC, explicit offsets, local time without a zone or monotonic counters.
prepare: Preserve original timestamps, source and record identifiers. Decide how to handle missing zones, precision, daylight-saving ambiguity and suspected clock skew.
workflow: Normalize only timestamps with justified timezone information. Sort by normalized time while keeping original values. Correlate independent sources and annotate uncertainty.
limits: Equal timestamps do not establish simultaneous activity or order. A correct timezone conversion does not correct an inaccurate source clock. Never silently assign a zone to ambiguous evidence.
tools: The supplied Python exercise rejects timestamps without an offset and preserves original record order for ties. Plaso/Timesketch support larger workflows when configured and validated.

title: Triage, searching and indicator interpretation
concept: Triage prioritizes evidence relevant to a question. Hash matches, keyword hits and pattern rules are leads whose meaning depends on the source and context.
prepare: Choose a small question-driven search set and document rule versions. Do not upload private evidence to public analysis services merely to obtain a verdict.
workflow: Compare a match with surrounding data, file format and provenance. Preserve both matched content and the reasoning used to classify it. Use a known sample as a negative or positive control.
limits: A YARA match identifies a rule condition, not automatically maliciousness. A known-good hash set may reduce workload but cannot prove every remaining file is harmful.
tools: Hash tools, strings, YARA and Autopsy search modules support triage; use reviewed local rules and record coverage limits.

title: Forensic reporting and reproducibility
concept: Separate observations, interpretations and conclusions. A reader should be able to trace a claim to a source artifact and repeat the analysis on the same evidence.
prepare: Record evidence identifiers, hashes, tool versions, commands, timezone assumptions, parser failures and derived-output locations. Include alternative explanations.
workflow: Report the smallest evidence necessary, preserve sensitive full records separately and state confidence qualitatively with its basis. Have critical steps independently reviewed where appropriate.
limits: Do not overstate attribution, intent, recovery completeness or timestamp precision. A reproducible result can still be based on incomplete evidence or a wrong assumption.
tools: Use the supplied worksheet and offline lab report. Recheck original hashes after analysis and preserve derived files separately.
